content: Nystatin is an antifungal medication that is approved by the FDA for the treatment of various fungal infections, including candidal vulvovaginitis, skin candidiasis, cutaneous and mucocutaneous infections, gastrointestinal candidiasis (excluding esophageal involvement), and oropharyngeal candidiasis. Common side effects include skin irritation and hypersensitivity reactions. For adults, Nystatin is available in several formulations with specific dosing instructions: Cream: Apply liberally to the affected areas topically twice daily until the infection is fully healed. This formulation is not intended for systemic, oral, intravaginal, or ophthalmic use. Powder: Apply to candidal lesions topically 2 to 3 times daily until healing is complete. For fungal infections of the feet, footwear should also be dusted with the powder. Tablets: Administer 1 to 2 tablets (500,000 to 1,000,000 units) orally three times daily. Treatment should continue for at least 48 hours after clinical symptoms resolve. Oral Suspension: Administer 4 to 6 mL (400,000 to 600,000 units) orally four times daily. The suspension should be retained in the mouth as long as possible before swallowing. Treatment should continue for at least 48 hours after symptoms disappear. For HIV patients, the recommended duration of treatment is 7 to 14 days. For pediatric patients, the dosing is as follows: Cream: Apply liberally to the affected areas topically twice daily until healing is complete. Powder: Apply to candidal lesions topically 2 to 3 times daily until healing is complete. For fungal infections of the feet, footwear should also be dusted with the powder. Oral Suspension (Infants): Administer 2 mL (200,000 units) orally four times daily. Treatment should continue for at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve. Oral Suspension (Children): Administer 4 to 6 mL (400,000 to 600,000 units) orally four times daily. The suspension should be retained in the mouth as long as possible before swallowing. Treatment should continue for at least 48 hours after symptoms disappear. For HIV patients, the recommended duration of treatment is 7 to 14 days. Nystatin is contraindicated in patients with a known hypersensitivity to any of its components. It is not suitable for systemic, oral, intravaginal, or ophthalmic infections. Diagnostic methods such as KOH smears or cultures are recommended to confirm the diagnosis of candidiasis and rule out other infections. Patients should be instructed to use the medication as prescribed and to complete the full course of treatment, even if symptoms improve early. If irritation develops, they should notify their physician promptly. If there is no therapeutic response, diagnostic tests should be repeated. Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include allergic reactions, burning, itching, rash, eczema, and pain at the application site, though these occur in less than 0.1% of cases. Nystatin is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA, meaning that animal reproduction studies have not been conducted, and it is unknown whether the drug can harm a fetus. It should only be prescribed to pregnant women if the potential benefit outweighs the potential risk. It is also unknown whether Nystatin is excreted in human breast milk, so caution is advised when prescribing it to nursing mothers. The safety and efficacy of Nystatin have been established in pediatric patients from birth to 16 years of age. However, there is limited data on its use in geriatric patients, and no specific guidance exists regarding its use in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, or in specific gender or racial populations. Nystatin is a polyene antifungal antibiotic derived from Streptomyces noursei. It works by binding to sterols in the fungal cell membrane, altering its permeability and causing leakage of intracellular components. Resistance to Nystatin is rare in Candida albicans, but other species of Candida may develop resistance during treatment, which is reversible upon discontinuation of the drug. Nystatin is not absorbed through intact skin or mucous membranes. It is fungistatic and fungicidal against a variety of yeasts and yeast-like fungi, including Candida albicans, C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis, and others. It has no activity against bacteria, protozoa, or viruses. No long-term studies have been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic, mutagenic, or fertility-impairing potential of Nystatin. It is available in various formulations, including creams, powders, and oral suspensions, and should be stored at 20-25°C (68-77°F).
